ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The following information applies for the next two problems. A circuit has a power source of $\mathcal{E}=5.82 \mathrm{~V}$ connected to three elements in series: an inductor with $L=12.5 \mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor with $C=48.5 \mu \mathrm{F}$, and a diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}=0.65 \mathrm{~V}$. (Of course, the polarity of the diode is aligned with that of the power source.) You close the switch, and after some time, the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant. (Note: An ideal diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}$ is one whose IV characteristic is given by $I=0$ for $V<V_{0}$ and $V=V_{0}$ for $I>0$.)

<image_1>

How much time (in seconds) has elapsed before the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a single series circuit. At the top, an inductor L, a capacitor C, and a diode can be seen in sequence; at the bottom there is a power supply and a switch. The direction of the diode is consistent with the polarity of the power supply, so after the switch is closed, the initial current direction will make the diode conduct in the forward direction. Reasoning: Take the given parameters E=5.82 V, V0=0.65 V, L=12.5 mH=12.5×10^-3 H, C=48.5 μF=48.5×10^-6 F. The capacitor is initially uncharged, and just when the switch is closed, q(0)=0, I(0)=0. During the diode conduction period, it can be equivalently regarded as a fixed voltage drop V0, so the series circuit satisfies KVL: L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E, and I=dq/dt. Thus there is L d²q/dt² + q/C = E - V0. The solution of this forced LC equation under the initial conditions q(0)=0 and I(0)=0 is q/C = (E - V0)(1 - cos(ωt)), I = C(E - V0)ω sin(ωt), where ω=1/sqrt(LC). The moment when the capacitor voltage becomes constant is the moment when the current first returns to 0 and the diode stops conducting, that is, the first nonzero solution of sin(ωt)=0: t=π/ω=πsqrt(LC). Substituting L=12.5×10^-3 H, C=48.5×10^-6 F: t=πsqrt((12.5×10^-3)(48.5×10^-6))=2.446×10^-3 s.

method.method_draft: Use the diagram to identify a single series loop containing the battery, inductor, capacitor, and forward-oriented threshold diode. From the text take E=5.82 V, V0=0.65 V, L=12.5 mH, C=48.5 microF, with the capacitor initially uncharged and switch just closed. While the diode conducts, replace it by a fixed voltage drop V0, so KVL gives L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E, with I=dq/dt, q(0)=0, I(0)=0. Solve the driven LC equation: q/C = (E-V0)(1-cos(omega t)), I = C(E-V0) omega sin(omega t), where omega=1/sqrt(LC). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first returns to zero and the diode stops conducting, i.e. sin(omega t)=0 at the first nonzero time t=pi/omega=pi sqrt(LC). Substitute L=12.5e-3 H and C=48.5e-6 F to get t=2.446e-3 s.

method.method_draft: Use the image to recognize that after the switch closes the forward diode allows only the first charging half-cycle of the lossless LC series circuit; once the inductor current would reverse, the diode blocks and the capacitor is isolated at constant voltage. From the text, during conduction the battery plus threshold diode provide a constant effective drive E-V0 across the LC pair. Shift the capacitor charge coordinate by the static equilibrium value q_eq=C(E-V0). The variable x=q-q_eq obeys the undriven SHO equation x''+x/(LC)=0. Initially q=0 and I=0, so the system starts at one turning point relative to the shifted equilibrium. The capacitor becomes constant at the next turning point, when I=0 again and the diode cuts off, which is half an LC period later. Therefore t=T/2=pi sqrt(LC). Numerically, pi sqrt((12.5e-3)(48.5e-6))=2.446e-3 s.
method.CoT_raw:
Image description: The attached circuit diagram shows a single series loop containing a battery/power source, a switch, an inductor labeled L, a capacitor labeled C, and a diode. The diode is oriented so that the battery polarity drives current through it in the forward direction after the switch is closed.

Reasoning: Since the diode is forward-biased by the source initially, current flows only during the first charging part of the LC motion. During conduction, the diode has a fixed threshold drop V0, so the LC pair is driven by the constant effective voltage E − V0. Let q be the capacitor charge and I = dq/dt. The circuit equation during conduction is L q'' + q/C = E − V0. Define q_eq = C(E − V0) and x = q − q_eq. Then x satisfies x'' + x/(LC) = 0. Initially, the capacitor is uncharged and the inductor current is zero, so q(0)=0 and I(0)=0; relative to the shifted equilibrium this is a turning point. The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current next reaches zero, because after that the LC current would reverse but the diode blocks reverse current. The next turning point occurs after half an LC period: t = T/2 = π sqrt(LC). Substituting L = 12.5e-3 H and C = 48.5e-6 F gives t = π sqrt((12.5e-3)(48.5e-6)) = 2.446e-3 s.

ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The following information applies for the next two problems. A circuit has a power source of $\mathcal{E}=5.82 \mathrm{~V}$ connected to three elements in series: an inductor with $L=12.5 \mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor with $C=48.5 \mu \mathrm{F}$, and a diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}=0.65 \mathrm{~V}$. The polarity of the diode is aligned with that of the power source. You close the switch, and after some time, the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant. (Note: An ideal diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}$ is one whose IV characteristic is given by $I=0$ for $V<V_{0}$ and $V=V_{0}$ for $I>0$.) How much time (in seconds) has elapsed before the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The figure shows a single series circuit. At the top, an inductor L, a capacitor C, and a diode can be seen in sequence; at the bottom there is a power supply and a switch. The direction of the diode is consistent with the polarity of the power supply, so after the switch is closed, the initial current direction will make the diode conduct in the forward direction.

Reasoning: Take the given parameters E=5.82 V, V0=0.65 V, L=12.5 mH=12.5×10^-3 H, C=48.5 μF=48.5×10^-6 F. The capacitor is initially uncharged, and just when the switch is closed, q(0)=0, I(0)=0. During the diode conduction period, it can be equivalently regarded as a fixed voltage drop V0, so the series circuit satisfies KVL: L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E, and I=dq/dt. Thus there is L d²q/dt² + q/C = E - V0. The solution of this forced LC equation under the initial conditions q(0)=0 and I(0)=0 is q/C = (E - V0)(1 - cos(ωt)), I = C(E - V0)ω sin(ωt), where ω=1/sqrt(LC). The moment when the capacitor voltage becomes constant is the moment when the current first returns to 0 and the diode stops conducting, that is, the first nonzero solution of sin(ωt)=0: t=π/ω=πsqrt(LC). Substituting L=12.5×10^-3 H, C=48.5×10^-6 F: t=πsqrt((12.5×10^-3)(48.5×10^-6))=2.446×10^-3 s.
